title: BEFORE vs AFTER Triggers & Audit Logging
description: Sanitize data before writing with BEFORE triggers and record audit trails with AFTER triggers.

data.text: **`BEFORE` triggers** execute before row data is written to disk, allowing you to sanitize, normalize, or reject the operation by returning `NEW` or `NULL`. **`AFTER` triggers** run after data has been persisted, making them ideal for audit trails and notification dispatching.

data.title: Automated Audit Logging with AFTER Trigger
data.content: Recording historical changes to customer records.
data.code:
-- 1. Trigger Function
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION log_customer_changes()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO customer_audit_log (
        customer_id, 
        operation, 
        changed_by, 
        old_data, 
        new_data
    )
    VALUES (
        COALESCE(NEW.id, OLD.id),
        TG_OP,
        current_user,
        to_jsonb(OLD),
        to_jsonb(NEW)
    );
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- 2. Bind AFTER Trigger
CREATE TRIGGER trg_customer_audit
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON customers
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_customer_changes();

data.text: A row-level trigger runs once per affected row, so a statement that updates a million rows calls it a million times. A statement-level trigger runs once for the whole statement and uses transition tables (`REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS ...`) to see every affected row at once, which is far cheaper for bulk operations.

data.title: Auditing a whole statement in one call
data.content: The transition table `changed` holds every row the UPDATE touched; the trigger writes one audit row per changed record in a single INSERT.
data.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION audit_bulk_change()
RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO orders_audit (operation, order_id, changed_at)
    SELECT TG_OP, order_id, now()
    FROM changed;

    RETURN NULL;
END $$;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_audit_bulk
AFTER UPDATE ON orders
REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS changed
FOR EACH STATEMENT
EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_bulk_change();

data.title: Choose BEFORE to mutate, AFTER to react
data.text: Use `BEFORE` when you need to change the row that is about to be written or reject it by returning `NULL`. Use `AFTER` when the write has already happened and you want to log it, update a summary table, or notify another system. A `BEFORE` trigger that returns `NULL` silently cancels the row, which is easy to miss during debugging.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `BEFORE` triggers to modify `NEW` columns before writing to disk.
Use `AFTER` triggers for audit tables and foreign key side-effects.
